canonicalExplanation.summary: An **issue** is a request for work that someone else can pick up without asking you twenty questions. A good one has: a **specific title**, the **context** (version, browser or OS), **steps to reproduce**, **expected vs actual** behaviour, **acceptance criteria** (how we'll know it's done), and **evidence** such as a log excerpt, screenshot or tiny test case. Keep it to **one problem**. And **never paste secrets or personal data**: redact tokens, passwords, emails and customer details, because issues are often public and are kept forever.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner reports a bug titled "cart broken". Three days later nobody has touched it: the maintainer can't reproduce it and doesn't know what "broken" means. A bug issue includes minimal reproduction steps, version, expected total, actual total, and a redacted test case while omitting customer data. In this lesson you'll write a scoped issue that another learner can understand and verify.

```predict
{"question": "Which title helps a maintainer most?", "options": ["Cart broken!!", "Cart total ignores discount when quantity is 0"], "answer": 1, "why": "A specific title states the behaviour and condition, and is searchable."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Remotes and synchronization**, **Inputs, outputs and constraints** (inputs, outputs and expected results) and **Diffs and patch review**.

sections.heading: The model: an issue someone else can verify
sections.body:
```markdown
### Cart total ignores discount when quantity is 0

**Version:** v1.4.2, Chrome 128, Windows 11

**Steps to reproduce**
1. Add item "Pen" (price 10.00), set quantity to 0.
2. Apply code SAVE10.

**Expected:** total 0.00
**Actual:** total -1.00

**Test case (redacted):** `total([{price: 10, qty: 0}], "SAVE10")` returns -1.

**Acceptance criteria**
- [ ] Total is never negative.
- [ ] A regression test covers qty 0 with a discount.
```

| Include | Leave out |
|---|---|
| version and environment. | API keys, tokens, passwords. |
| minimal reproduction steps. | customer names, emails, addresses. |
| expected vs actual. | several unrelated bugs in one issue. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why a minimal test case instead of the whole customer order?", "answer": "It isolates the cause, anyone can run it, and it contains no personal data."}
```

sections.heading: One issue, one problem

includes: Write issues with context, reproduction steps, expected vs actual behaviour and acceptance criteria.
Redact secrets and personal data, and keep each issue to one problem.

outcomes: Write a scoped issue that another learner can understand and verify.

examples.title: The wrong cart total
examples.situation: A bug issue includes minimal reproduction steps, version, expected total, actual total, and a redacted test case while omitting customer data.
walkthrough: **Minimal reproduction steps and version:** two steps, v1.4.2, Chrome on Windows.
**A redacted test case while omitting customer data:** one line of input that fails; the customer's name and email are removed, so anyone will be able to verify the fix.
examples.result: A teammate reproduces the bug in two minutes and knows exactly when it's fixed.

examples.title: The feature request with no finish line
examples.situation: An issue says "Make search better". Two people work on it and disagree about whether it's done.
walkthrough: Rewrite as a specific need: "Search should match partial words".
Add acceptance criteria: "'calc' finds 'calculator'; results appear under 300 ms".
Split other search ideas into their own issues.
examples.result: Everyone agrees on the goal and on when the issue can be closed.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: A short title such as login broken is enough because developers can discover the environment and expected behavior themselves.
misconceptions.correction: Without environment, steps and expected behaviour, others must guess or ask, and bugs that can't be reproduced often go unfixed.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening story, why had nobody touched the "cart broken" issue?

analogy.example: An issue is like **a note to a mechanic**. "Car broken" gets a shrug. "Squeal from front left when braking above 50 km/h, since Tuesday" gets it fixed. You'd also never leave your house keys taped to the note: that's the secret you redact.
usefulFor: never tape keys to the note
limitations: Mechanics can inspect the car; maintainers often can't see your machine.
Acceptance criteria are the "squeal is gone" test drive.

nearTransfer.prompt: Rewrite this issue so someone else could verify it: "Login broken on my laptop, pls fix asap. my token is ghp_abc123".

farTransfer.prompt: Find a real small bug or missing feature in one of your projects. Write the issue with title, environment, steps, expected/actual, evidence and acceptance criteria. Ask a partner to reproduce it using only the issue.

remediation.explanation: Before submitting, read the issue as a stranger: **could I reproduce this, and would I know when it's fixed?** Then scan for **anything secret or personal**.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The feature request with no finish line".

recap.summary: To write a scoped issue another learner can verify, give it a specific title, the version and environment, minimal steps, expected and actual behaviour, evidence and acceptance criteria, keep it to one problem, and redact all secrets and personal data.
